analysis.one_liner: Nullifies the rule requiring lenders to disclose more detail about home mortgages.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it drew zero cosponsors, got no vote, and the expanded mortgage-disclosure rule stayed in force.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would erase, by act of Congress, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2015 update to the Home Mortgage Disclosure rule. That update requires mortgage lenders to report more information about the loans they make — data regulators and the public use to spot discrimination and risky lending. The bill would have taken the whole rule off the books.
analysis.who_benefits: Mortgage lenders. The bill would relieve them of the expanded reporting the 2015 rule added — fewer data points to collect, verify, and submit each year [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that the CFPB's 2015 'Home Mortgage Disclosure (Regulation C)' rule 'shall have no force or effect,' wiping out the rule entirely rather than amending it [S3].
The nullified rule is the one that expanded the scope of information financial institutions must disclose about home mortgages, so the bill would return lenders to lighter reporting duties [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Homebuyers and the neighborhoods they live in. The mortgage data at issue is what regulators, researchers, and community groups use to detect discriminatory or predatory lending. Losing it would make that scrutiny harder, with no replacement [S2].

drawbacks.text: The 2015 rule added real reporting work: lenders have to collect and submit additional data points on each mortgage application, a cost that falls hardest on smaller institutions [S2].

Defenders of lighter reporting argue that some of the expanded data goes beyond what regulators demonstrably need, so the compliance burden is not free. The bill offered no way to trim the rule while keeping the core public data — it deleted everything at once [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings for lenders come entirely from making less information public. The data behind mortgage disclosure is the main tool for detecting lending discrimination by neighborhood, race, and income, so the public cost is a weaker ability to see where discrimination and risky lending happen. The bill offered no narrower alternative, only full repeal of the rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was filed, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, the first day of the 117th Congress [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
Because the bill died, the 2015 mortgage-disclosure rule remained in effect [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuyers, community groups, and fair-lending regulators kept the expanded public mortgage data, since the rule was never erased. Lenders continue to bear the reporting costs the rule imposes.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to nullify the 2015 mortgage-disclosure rule.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no bipartisan movement in either direction [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have freed lenders from the expanded data-reporting duties of the 2015 rule. That gain is paid for by the public: the same data is what lets regulators and researchers detect discriminatory and predatory lending.

industries.industry: Fair-lending enforcement and community advocacy groups
industries.note: These groups rely on mortgage-disclosure data to identify lending discrimination and hold lenders accountable; erasing the rule would strip their main dataset.
